scorecard.note: Beats 1 and 3 repeat the same fact (counts fell by about half or more) in a row, and the numbers don't line up. '101' has no unit, 'under half' conflicts with the 62% drop, and the 2.6% a year pace is never tied to a baseline. Rebuild it as

storyboard.ears: Men today have about half the sperm their grandfathers did.
In 1973, the average count was 101. By 2018 it was under half that, so grandfathers had the edge.
storyboard.evidence: Human Reproduction Update | Average sperm concentration, 1973 vs 2018 (million per mL) | https://academic.oup.com/humupd/article/29/2/157/6932384 | 2026-11-05

storyboard.ears: Since 2000, counts fall 2.6% a year, more than double the old pace. The drop itself is speeding up.
storyboard.evidence: Human Reproduction Update | Annual rate of sperm count decline, before vs after 2000 (percent per year) | https://academic.oup.com/humupd/article/29/2/157/6932384 | 2026-11-05

storyboard.ears: Total sperm count fell 62%, even worse than concentration. Men now make far fewer sperm overall, not just thinner samples.
storyboard.evidence: Human Reproduction Update | Decline in sperm concentration vs total sperm count, 1973-2018 (percent) | https://academic.oup.com/humupd/article/29/2/157/6932384 | 2026-11-05

storyboard.ears: It's speeding up, and sperm counts matter for any family hoping to have kids.
